Obscurantism is the deliberate practice of keeping people confused, ignorant, or in the dark — either by blocking the spread of knowledge, or by making things unnecessarily difficult to understand. The key word here is deliberate. It is never an accident. Someone practicing obscurantism is choosing, on purpose, to muddy the waters.

Think of it this way: imagine someone who knows the answer to your question, but instead of giving you a clear answer, they bury it under so much complicated jargon, vagueness, and noise that you walk away more confused than when you started — and they did it on purpose. That is obscurantism.

Obscurantism shows up in two major ways in real life, and it helps to understand both separately.

1. Political & Institutional Obscurantism

This is when those who hold power — governments, religious institutions, authoritarian rulers, corporations — deliberately prevent ordinary people from gaining knowledge, education, or access to the truth. The motive is almost always control. An uninformed population is easier to rule. People who don't understand their rights, the law, or the workings of power are far less likely to challenge it.

Historical examples of this include:

  • Governments that banned certain books, burned libraries, or censored newspapers so that citizens couldn't form independent opinions.
  • Institutions that kept sacred texts in languages ordinary people could not read, ensuring that only a privileged few could interpret and control what those texts "meant."
  • Regimes that deliberately under-funded public education in certain regions or communities to keep those populations dependent and easy to manipulate.

In all these cases, the people in power are not failing to educate — they are actively working against education and clarity. That active, intentional suppression of knowledge is obscurantism.

2. Intellectual & Academic Obscurantism

This form lives in the world of writing, philosophy, academia, and public debate. It happens when a thinker, writer, or speaker uses deliberately complex, vague, or convoluted language — not to explain something genuinely difficult, but to:

  • Hide the fact that their argument is weak or empty.
  • Make themselves appear more intelligent or profound than they actually are.
  • Avoid being challenged or held accountable, because if nobody can understand what you said, nobody can prove you wrong.

Here is a simple illustration. Compare these two sentences:

Clear version: "People behave better when they feel they are being watched."

Obscurantist version: "The performative recalibration of behavioral paradigms under conditions of perceived panoptic surveillance constitutes a dialectical instantiation of socially constructed normative compliance."

Both sentences are saying roughly the same thing. But the second one is dressed in so much unnecessary complexity that most readers feel either intimidated or impressed — when in reality, the idea itself is straightforward. If someone consistently writes or speaks like the second sentence when the first would do just fine, they are practicing intellectual obscurantism.
The One Thing That Defines Obscurantism: Intent

This is crucial. Obscurantism is not the same as something simply being hard to understand. Quantum physics is hard to understand, but that is because it describes genuinely complex phenomena — not because physicists are trying to confuse you. A legal contract can be dense and difficult, but that difficulty might arise from the need for precision, not from a desire to deceive.

Obscurantism requires bad faith. There must be a deliberate choice to obscure, confuse, or withhold. The moment that intent is present — the moment someone is using complexity or silence as a weapon or a shield — you have obscurantism.

Ask yourself: Is this person being unclear because the subject demands it, or because they benefit from me not understanding it? The answer tells you whether you are looking at genuine complexity or obscurantism.

People and institutions resort to obscurantism for a handful of consistent reasons:

  • To maintain power. Knowledge is power. Denying people knowledge keeps power concentrated at the top.
  • To avoid accountability. If your argument is unclear enough, no one can pin you down on it.
  • To appear superior. In academic and intellectual circles, impenetrable writing can be mistaken for deep thinking, granting the writer undeserved status.
  • To protect vested interests. Industries, ideologies, and institutions sometimes deliberately confuse the public about inconvenient facts — think of how some companies have historically funded misleading research to cloud public understanding of topics that threatened their business.
How to Recognize Obscurantism in Real Life

Once you understand this word, you will start noticing it everywhere. Here are signs that you may be encountering it:

  • Unnecessary jargon used in a context where plain language would work perfectly well.
  • Vague or circular answers to direct questions — lots of words that somehow say nothing.
  • Gatekeeping of information — knowledge kept in exclusive languages, paywalls, or elite circles with no good reason.
  • Attacks on education or critical thinking framed as tradition, loyalty, or virtue.
  • The "too complicated for you" dismissal — when someone tells you an issue is far too complex for ordinary people to understand, and that you should simply trust the experts (without explaining anything).

The natural opposite of obscurantism is enlightenment — the belief that knowledge should be spread freely, that ideas should be expressed as clearly as possible, and that ordinary people are capable of understanding the world around them if given the chance. Where obscurantism thrives on confusion and gatekeeping, the enlightenment tradition thrives on clarity, transparency, and the democratization of knowledge.

Obscurantism is the deliberate act of keeping people ignorant or confused, either by suppressing knowledge and education at a societal level, or by burying ideas under unnecessary complexity in writing and speech. It is always intentional, and it almost always serves someone's interest in maintaining power, prestige, or avoiding scrutiny. Recognizing it is one of the most useful intellectual skills you can develop, because once you can identify when someone is working against your understanding rather than for it, you become far harder to manipulate.
